title: find() returns a cursor, not documents
question: When find() 'returns documents,' what is it actually returning?
answer: A cursor to the matching documents -- not the documents themselves. You iterate the cursor to actually access them.

title: Type bracketing in comparisons
question: If a 'qty' field holds a string value "fourteen" in one document, does { qty: { $gt: 4 } } match it?
answer: No. Comparison operators only compare documents where the field's BSON type matches the query operand's type (numeric types are an exception and convert before comparing) -- a string never matches a numeric $gt.

title: mongosh auto-iterates the first 20 results
question: In mongosh, if you run db.collection.find() without assigning it to a variable, how many documents get displayed automatically?
answer: Up to the first 20 documents -- the cursor is automatically iterated. Type 'it' to continue iteration further.

title: Comparison operators live inside the filter
question: In PyMongo, where do comparison operators like $gt and $ne go relative to the field name?
answer: Nested one level inside the field's value: { "field": { "$gt": value } } -- the same query-filter shape mongosh uses, since PyMongo speaks the same MQL.

title: Dot notation for embedded fields in a filter
question: How do you query on a field nested inside an embedded document, e.g. name.last, in a find() filter?
answer: Dot notation: { "name.last": "Hopper" } -- the embedded field path as a single quoted string key.

title: Empty filter returns every document
question: What filter do you pass to find() to return every document in a collection?
answer: An empty document: find({}) (or find() with no argument in mongosh) -- omitting or emptying the filter matches all documents.

title: Logical operators combine multiple clauses
question: Which logical operators combine multiple query clauses in a find() filter, and what does each do?
answer: $and (all clauses must match), $or (at least one clause matches), $nor (no clause matches), and $not (negates a single expression).

title: find_one() return value
question: What does PyMongo's find_one() return if one or more documents match, versus if none match?
answer: The first matching document as a Python dictionary if any match; None if no documents match the filter.

title: When to reach for find_one()
question: When is find_one() the right choice instead of find()?
answer: When you know there's only one matching document, or you're only interested in the first match -- it skips creating and iterating a cursor for the rest.

title: find_one() with no sort criteria
question: If you don't specify sort criteria, in what order does find_one() pick which document to return?
answer: Natural order on disk -- whichever matching document happens to come first in the collection's storage order, not necessarily insertion or any logical order.

title: ObjectId from a URL string
question: A web app receives a document's ObjectId as a string in a URL path. Can you pass that string directly to find_one({'_id': ...})?
answer: No -- you must convert it to an ObjectId instance first (e.g. ObjectId(id_string)) before passing it to find_one(); a raw string won't match the stored ObjectId value.

title: Customizing find_one()/find() behavior
question: Name three named arguments you can pass to find_one()/find() to customize its behavior.
answer: Examples include max_time_ms (execution time limit), hint (index to use), comment (attached to the operation), collation (string comparison rules), and batch_size (cursor batching).

title: Can't mix include and exclude
question: Can a single projection document both include some fields (1) and exclude other fields (0) at the same time?
answer: No -- except for _id, which can always be explicitly excluded (0) from an otherwise-inclusive projection, or explicitly included (1) in an otherwise-exclusive one.

title: _id is included by default
question: If your projection only lists fields to include (e.g. { name: 1 }), is _id returned too?
answer: Yes -- _id is returned by default in an inclusion projection unless you explicitly suppress it with _id: 0.

title: $slice for array elements
question: How do you project just the last element of an array field instead of the whole array?
answer: Use the $slice projection operator, e.g. { "instock": { "$slice": -1 } } -- a negative value slices from the end of the array.

title: Projecting a field inside an embedded document
question: How do you project only the 'uom' field from a nested 'size' embedded document, without returning the rest of 'size'?
answer: Dot notation in the projection: { "size.uom": 1 } -- returns just that one nested field rather than the whole embedded document.

title: You can't project an array element by index
question: Can you project just the first element of an array field using its index, e.g. { "instock.0": 1 }?
answer: No -- that does not project the array's first element. Only $elemMatch, $slice, and the positional $ operator can select specific array elements in a projection.

title: Projections can compute new fields
question: Can a find() projection do more than just include/exclude existing fields -- e.g. compute a brand-new field value?
answer: Yes -- using aggregation expressions and syntax (like $switch, $concat, $literal) in the projection document, you can project new computed fields or override the value of existing ones.

title: Why cursors exist
question: Why does PyMongo return a cursor instead of all matching documents at once for a multi-document read?
answer: A cursor returns results in iterable batches, holding only a subset of documents in memory at any time -- reducing memory consumption and network bandwidth compared to fetching everything at once.

title: Iterating a cursor
question: What's the standard way to access every document in a PyMongo cursor?
answer: A for loop directly over the cursor object (for doc in results: ...) -- or async for in the asynchronous API.

title: Risk of list(cursor)
question: What's the risk of calling list(cursor) to convert a PyMongo cursor into a list?
answer: It loads every matching document into memory at once -- if the result set is large, this can exceed available application memory and crash the program. Iterate large result sets instead.

title: Cursor closing
question: When does MongoDB close a cursor by default, and how can you close one early?
answer: By default, MongoDB closes a cursor once the client has exhausted all its results. You can close one explicitly with close(), or use a 'with' block so PyMongo closes it automatically when the block ends.

title: Tailable cursors
question: What is a tailable cursor, and what kind of collection does it require?
answer: A cursor that remains open after the client exhausts the current results (e.g. for tailing the oplog) -- created by specifying CursorType.TAILABLE_AWAIT, and only usable on a capped collection.

title: limit() must come before retrieval
question: When must you apply limit() to a cursor relative to when you start retrieving documents?
answer: Before retrieving any documents from the database -- limit() has no effect if applied after documents have already started being fetched.

title: limit(0) means no limit
question: What does calling .limit(0) on a cursor do?
answer: Nothing -- a limit() value of 0 is equivalent to setting no limit at all, not zero results.

title: Negative limit closes after one batch
question: How does a negative limit value (e.g. .limit(-5)) behave differently from a positive one?
answer: It's similar to a positive limit, but the server closes the cursor after returning a single batch of results -- the client won't request a subsequent batch via getMore, so fewer documents than the limit may come back if they don't fit in one batch.

title: skip()/limit() chaining order doesn't matter
question: Does the order you chain .skip() and .limit() (skip-then-limit vs. limit-then-skip) change the query results?
answer: No -- the server always applies the skip operation (based on sort order) before applying the limit, regardless of the order you wrote them in the chain.

title: skip() gets slower as the offset grows
question: Why does skip()-based pagination get slower as the page offset increases, and what's the documented alternative?
answer: skip() requires the server to scan from the beginning of the result set before it can start returning results, so larger offsets mean more scanning. Range queries (filtering on the last-seen value with $gt/$lt) avoid this and typically perform better as the offset grows.

title: sort() needs a unique tiebreaker for consistency
question: If you sort on a field containing duplicate values, is the relative order of the duplicate-valued documents guaranteed to be the same across repeated executions?
answer: No -- $sort is not a stable sort, so documents with equivalent sort keys can come back in any order. Include a field with exclusively unique values (like _id) in the sort to guarantee a consistent order.

title: Sort key for an array-valued field
question: When sorting on a field that holds an array, what value does MongoDB actually use as the sort key?
answer: In an ascending sort, the lowest value in the array; in a descending sort, the highest value in the array -- and this is true regardless of which array elements matched the query filter.

title: BSON type comparison order
question: When sorting a field that mixes numbers and strings across documents, which values sort first: the numbers or the strings?
answer: Numbers sort first (lower) than strings. MongoDB's overall comparison order, low to high, is roughly: MinKey, Null, Numbers, Symbol/String, Object, Array, BinData, ObjectId, Boolean, Date, Timestamp, Regex, JavaScript, JavaScript with scope, MaxKey.

title: Counting all documents
question: How do you get an accurate count of every document in a collection with count_documents()?
answer: Pass an empty filter: collection.count_documents({}) -- an empty dictionary matches (and counts) every document.

title: count() is deprecated
question: What happens if you call Cursor.count() in a current version of PyMongo?
answer: It raises an AttributeError -- PyMongo no longer supports the old count() method. Use count_documents() on the Collection class instead.

title: estimated_document_count() vs count_documents()
question: How does estimated_document_count() differ from count_documents(), and why might it be faster?
answer: It estimates the document count from collection metadata instead of actually counting matching documents, which can be faster -- but it doesn't accept a query filter, so it only estimates the total collection size, not a filtered subset.

title: Customizing count_documents()
question: Name two optional parameters count_documents() accepts to customize the count operation.
answer: Examples include skip, limit, maxTimeMS, hint, collation, and comment -- if none are specified, the count runs without any customization.

title: insertOne() return document shape
question: What does a successful db.collection.insertOne() call return?
answer: A document with acknowledged (true if it ran with write concern) and insertedId (the _id value of the inserted document).

title: insertOne() auto-creates the collection
question: What happens if you call insertOne() on a collection that doesn't exist yet?
answer: MongoDB creates the collection automatically before inserting the document -- no separate create-collection step is needed.

title: insertOne() and explain()
question: Can you run db.collection.explain() on an insertOne() call?
answer: No -- insertOne() is not compatible with explain(); it isn't a query operation whose plan can be explained.

title: insertOne() error types
question: What kind of error does insertOne() throw when a write fails?
answer: Either a writeError (e.g. a duplicate _id) or a writeConcernError (e.g. the requested write concern couldn't be satisfied in time).

title: Duplicate _id on insertOne()
question: What happens if you insertOne() a document whose _id value already exists in the collection?
answer: MongoDB throws a WriteError with code 11000 (duplicate key error) and the document is not inserted.

title: insert_one() Python parameters
question: What optional parameters does PyMongo's insert_one() accept?
answer: bypass_document_validation (skip schema validation, defaults to False), session (a ClientSession), and comment -- if none are given, the insert is not customized.

title: insertMany() return document shape
question: What does a successful db.collection.insertMany() call return?
answer: A document with an acknowledged boolean and an insertedIds array containing the _id of each successfully inserted document.

title: ordered vs unordered insertMany()
question: How does the ordered option change what happens when one document in an insertMany() batch fails to insert?
answer: With ordered:true (the default), the server stops inserting as soon as one document fails. With ordered:false, the server skips the failure and keeps inserting the remaining documents.

title: insertMany() batching limit
question: Is there a limit to how many documents you can pass to a single insertMany() call?
answer: No hard limit -- the driver internally batches documents according to maxWriteBatchSize (100,000, not configurable), so a 250,000-document call becomes three batches (two of 100,000, one of 50,000).

title: insertMany() error type
question: What exception type does insertMany() throw on a write failure, as opposed to insertOne()?
answer: A BulkWriteError, not the writeError/writeConcernError that insertOne() throws -- it reports successful counts plus per-document errors.

title: insertMany() oplog consolidation
question: Does a successful insertMany() of 100 documents create 100 separate oplog entries?
answer: No -- MongoDB consolidates a multi-document insert (insertMany(), or several insertOne()s inside one bulkWrite()) into a single oplog entry.

title: insert_many() extra ordered parameter
question: Besides the parameters insert_one() accepts, what extra option does PyMongo's insert_many() take?
answer: ordered (default True) -- when True, the driver sends documents in the given order and cancels any remaining inserts as soon as one fails.

title: Why let the driver generate _id
question: Why does PyMongo recommend letting the driver auto-generate the _id field instead of specifying your own value?
answer: To guarantee uniqueness -- a duplicate _id value violates the collection's unique index constraint and causes the driver to return an error.

title: _id's role as primary key
question: What role does the _id field play in a standard MongoDB collection?
answer: It acts as the document's required, unique primary key -- if a document omits it, the driver automatically generates an ObjectId for it.

title: Auto _id generation also applies to upserts
question: Does the automatic ObjectId-generation rule for a missing _id also apply to documents created via an upsert (upsert: true)?
answer: Yes -- if a document created through an upsert doesn't specify _id, the driver auto-generates an ObjectId for it, exactly as it would for a normal insert.

title: The $type "number" alias
question: What BSON type alias does $type support for matching any numeric value (integer, decimal, double, or long) in one query?
answer: The number alias. {field: {$type: "number"}} matches Int32, Int64 ("long"), Double, and Decimal128 fields in one query, instead of listing each numeric type separately.

title: ObjectId ordering guarantee
question: Are ObjectId values guaranteed to sort in exact creation order?
answer: No, only approximately. ObjectIds have just 1 second of timestamp resolution, so IDs created in the same second aren't ordered, and the timestamp is set by each client's own clock, which can differ across machines.

title: Binary subtype 8 (sensitive data)
question: What happens when you store a value in a BSON Binary field with subtype 8?
answer: MongoDB treats it as sensitive data (e.g. a key or secret) and never logs the literal value -- logs show a ### placeholder instead.

title: decimal128 vs double
question: When should you use decimal128 instead of double?
answer: Whenever exact decimal precision matters (e.g. financial/banking calculations). double is binary floating point and can't represent many base-10 decimals exactly, while decimal128 stores up to 34 decimal digits of precision exactly.

title: Date vs internal Timestamp
question: What's the difference between the BSON Date type and the BSON internal Timestamp type?
answer: Date is a 64-bit millisecond count meant for application use. Timestamp is a separate internal type (seconds + an incrementing per-second ordinal) used for things like the oplog. Application code should use Date, not Timestamp.

title: Deprecated BSON types
question: Which BSON types in the reference table are marked deprecated?
answer: Undefined, DBPointer, Symbol, and JavaScript with scope.

title: String sort() and non-ASCII characters
question: Why can sort() on string fields sometimes look "wrong" for non-ASCII characters?
answer: sort() uses the C++ strcmp API internally -- a byte-wise comparison, not locale-aware collation -- so ordering of some international characters may not match what you'd intuitively expect.

title: _id type restrictions
question: Can a document's _id field be an array or a regular-expression value?
answer: No. _id may be any BSON type except an array, regex, or undefined.

title: Missing _id on insert
question: If you insert a document without an _id field, what happens?
answer: The MongoDB driver (or mongod, if the driver didn't) automatically generates an ObjectId and adds it as _id -- this also applies to upserts.

title: Dot notation for arrays and embedded docs
question: How do you access the third element of an array field, or a nested field inside an embedded document, in a query?
answer: Dot notation: "contribs.2" for the third array element (zero-based index), or "contact.phone.number" for a nested embedded field.

title: Maximum document size
question: What is the maximum size of a single BSON document?
answer: 16 mebibytes. Larger data must use the GridFS API instead of a single document.

title: Field order matters in query comparisons
question: Are two documents with fields {a:1, b:1} and {b:1, a:1} considered equal in a query comparison?
answer: No -- field order is significant when comparing whole documents in MongoDB, even though it wouldn't matter in a plain JS/JSON object.

title: _id is always stored first
question: If a document is inserted with _id listed as the second field, where does the server actually place it?
answer: The server always moves _id to be the first field in the stored document, regardless of the order fields were sent in.

title: Collections vs. relational tables
question: What's the closest relational-database equivalent to a MongoDB collection?
answer: A table -- collections are analogous to tables in relational databases -- but unlike a table, a collection has no fixed schema by default.

title: No shared schema by default
question: Do all documents in a MongoDB collection need to share the same fields and types?
answer: No -- by default, documents in a collection do not share a schema; fields and data types can vary freely across documents unless you explicitly add schema validation rules.

title: Collection UUID
question: What uniquely and immutably identifies a MongoDB collection, even across a replica set or sharded cluster?
answer: Its UUID -- every collection is assigned an immutable UUID that stays consistent across all replica set members and shards.

title: Implicit collection creation
question: What's the simplest way to create a new collection in mongosh?
answer: Just write to it -- e.g. db.myNewCollection.insertOne({x: 1}) creates the collection (and the database, if needed) automatically if neither already exists.
